title: Flammability limit of fuel droplets is lower in reduced gravity
statement: FLEX found that heptane and methanol droplets keep burning at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than in normal gravity, lower even than predicted.
safetyImplication: Earth-based standards for inert-gas fire suppressants may not give the same margin of safety on a spacecraft.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)
NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Cool flames keep burning after the visible flame goes out
statement: After the hot flame of a large alkane droplet went out, the droplet kept vaporizing for a long time in an almost invisible low-temperature 'cool flame', then stopped, leaving a cloud of fuel vapour.
safetyImplication: A fire that looks extinguished may still be reacting and producing fuel vapour, which matters for detection and re-ignition.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)
NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: The 'weaker flames in microgravity' safety margin does not hold with ventilation
statement: Tests in still air suggested materials are less flammable in microgravity, but that margin may not be valid in real spacecraft, where ventilation airflow strongly strengthens flames.
safetyImplication: Ventilation must be treated as a fire-strengthening factor when rating materials and designing cabins.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Some materials burn at lower oxygen in low airflow, in microgravity and partial gravity
statement: In the low-flow conditions of microgravity or partial gravity, some materials keep burning at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity.
safetyImplication: Oxygen limits measured in Earth tests can overestimate how much oxygen a material needs to burn on a spacecraft or habitat.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Materials ignite more easily in low gravity
statement: Without buoyancy, less heat is carried away from a material's surface by natural convection, so materials are easier to ignite in low gravity.
safetyImplication: Ignition sources (hot electronics, wiring faults) are a greater hazard in low gravity than Earth tests suggest.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: In slow airflow, flames can spread upstream, against the air
statement: In microgravity with low forced airflow, a flame on a thin fuel spreads upstream into the oncoming air, the opposite of normal gravity, where it always spreads downstream with the buoyant flow.
safetyImplication: Fire may move toward the ventilation inlet, so detector and suppressant placement cannot assume Earth-like spread direction.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)
NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Radiant heat from nearby sources makes materials ignite and spread faster
statement: Heat lost by radiation from a material's surface reduces its flammability, but heat radiated onto it from outside can make it ignite and spread faster.
safetyImplication: Hot surfaces or a nearby fire can turn a marginally flammable material into a spreading fire.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Flames survive at the lowest oxygen near spacecraft ventilation speeds
statement: For flame spread over solids, the lowest oxygen level that still supports a flame occurs at an airflow of about 10 cm/s, which is also where flames spread fastest, and is typical of spacecraft ventilation. At even lower speeds, radiative loss puts the flame out.
safetyImplication: Normal cabin ventilation sits near the worst case for material flammability.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Ignition is faster and needs less heat in sub-buoyant airflow
statement: Reduced-gravity aircraft tests found ignition times well below those in normal-gravity buoyant flows when the airflow was slower than buoyancy would cause, and a model showed the critical heat flux for ignition in microgravity can be as low as half the normal-gravity value.
safetyImplication: Heat sources that are safe on Earth may ignite materials on a spacecraft.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Three early fire-safety beliefs were proved wrong
statement: NASA research disproved three misconceptions: that a steady fire cannot exist in still microgravity air, that a fire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off, and that terrestrial fire tests are very conservative because reduced gravity is inherently safer.
safetyImplication: Fire-safety plans cannot rely on microgravity, or on switching off ventilation, to put fires out.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Earth smoke detectors look for the wrong particles in space
statement: Flames in microgravity produce particles of very different sizes, so detectors that sense fire particulates need different signatures; a terrestrial detector would be 'looking' for the wrong thing.
safetyImplication: Spacecraft smoke detectors must be designed and tested for microgravity smoke.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Smoke production in low gravity differs from predictions
statement: Gas-jet flame studies found that the onset of smoke production in low gravity is substantially different from normal gravity and contrary to earlier predictions, with different soot particle sizes.
safetyImplication: Smoke and soot models built on Earth data need low-gravity validation before they are used for detection or toxicity.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Spacecraft hold all three sides of the fire triangle, often with extra oxygen
statement: Crewed spacecraft necessarily contain fuel, oxygen and ignition sources, often run at a higher oxygen fraction than air, offer limited escape and tolerate almost no damage to life support.
safetyImplication: Fire prevention (materials and ignition control) is the first line of defence; there is nowhere to run.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Nitrogen sprayed on a fire in microgravity can make it stronger
statement: In BASS, a nitrogen suppressant jet aimed at a flame could entrain oxygen and actually strengthen the flame instead of putting it out.
safetyImplication: Where and how a crew aims an extinguisher in microgravity matters more than on Earth; a poorly aimed jet can feed the fire.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Flames react fast and dramatically to changes in airflow
statement: On a 2-cm-wide cotton-fiberglass fabric in opposed flow, BASS stepped the airflow down from 10 cm/s to below 1 cm/s; the flame and its spread rate changed very rapidly and dramatically with each step.
safetyImplication: Changing cabin ventilation during a fire immediately changes how fast it spreads.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Fires in orbit burned fuel-rich and produced much more carbon monoxide
statement: In BASS-II, CO to CO2 ratios were an order of magnitude higher than in efficient combustion; flames burned fuel-rich (global equivalence ratio about 1.3) under low-velocity flow, and most released well below 100 W.
safetyImplication: Even small fires in microgravity can be disproportionately toxic; CO monitoring matters as much as flame detection.

sources.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II (BASS-II) Summary Report (NASA/TM-20210011385)

title: A U-shaped flammability boundary: flames die at too little or too much airflow
statement: BASS-II crews adapted to new flow variations, including blowoff extinctions, which helped outline a U-shaped flammability boundary.
safetyImplication: Both very low and very high airflow can put a fire out; between them lies a band where materials burn best.

sources.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II (BASS-II) Summary Report (NASA/TM-20210011385)

title: NASA's ground material test may not be conservative for space
statement: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 rates materials with an upward flame spread test in normal gravity; drop-tower results suggest it might not be conservative for reduced gravity.
safetyImplication: Materials that pass Test 1 may still burn on a spacecraft; margins or a modified test are needed.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)
Organizing Questions for Reduced-Gravity Flammability

title: Large spacecraft fires reached 10 kW but cabin averages stayed acceptable
statement: Saffire IV and V burned 40-cm-wide samples inside a Cygnus spacecraft; fires with heat release up to 10 kW measurably changed cabin pressure, temperature and CO2, but average conditions did not rise to unacceptable levels.
safetyImplication: A crewed vehicle can survive a large fire's heat and pressure; the threat is local damage and the gases.

sources.title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

title: In a spacecraft fire, CO2 and CO rise matters more than heat and pressure
statement: In Saffire VI, the rise in spacecraft temperature and pressure was less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide.
safetyImplication: Toxic gas, not heat, is the main hazard to crew after a fire; detection and cleanup of CO and CO2 are critical.

sources.title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment (ICES-2024-365)

title: Spacecraft fire designs had to rely on 1 g knowledge
statement: Before Saffire, the lack of large-scale data forced spacecraft designers to base fire safety on 1 g understanding of flame spread, self-extinguishment, detection and suppression.
safetyImplication: Large-scale tests in microgravity are needed to replace Earth assumptions in vehicle design.

sources.title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment (ICES-2024-365)

title: Smoke particles from overheated spacecraft materials are mostly 200–400 nm
statement: SAME-2 heated five spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber, Pyrell) below ignition in airflow up to 8 cm/s; most average smoke particle sizes were 200–400 nm, with some much larger particles in still air.
safetyImplication: Spacecraft smoke detectors must sense particles in this size range, including from smouldering before any flame.

sources.title: Particle Morphology and Size Results from the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-2

title: Water-mist extinguishers replaced CO2 units on the ISS
statement: After years of research and flight experiments, water-mist portable fire extinguishers were certified for spaceflight; the first two of nine were sent to the ISS in December 2015 to replace CO2 units.
safetyImplication: Water mist is NASA's current direction for crew-operated suppression, avoiding the CO2 hazard in a closed cabin.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Candles burned for up to 45 minutes on Mir
statement: In still microgravity air, candle flames on Mir burned for as long as 45 minutes and to a lower oxygen level than the same candle would on Earth; on the Shuttle they lasted under 60 seconds because the candle box limited oxygen.
safetyImplication: A small, dim fire can persist for a long time in still air on a spacecraft and is easy to miss.

sources.title: Candle Flames in Non-Buoyant Atmospheres (Dietrich et al.)
NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: Flames oscillate before they go out
statement: Candle flames on the Shuttle and Mir showed spontaneous, symmetric oscillations just before extinction, which could last over a minute.
safetyImplication: A flickering, near-dead flame is not yet out; crews should confirm extinction.

sources.title: Candle Flames in Non-Buoyant Atmospheres (Dietrich et al.)
NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: The weakest flames ever burned exist only in microgravity
statement: SOFBALL showed stationary spherical 'flame balls' can exist in lean premixed gases in microgravity, the weakest flames ever burned (about 1 watt), some burning for over 40 minutes.
safetyImplication: Very lean gas mixtures that could not burn on Earth may sustain tiny flames in microgravity.

sources.title: NASA, Combustion in Reduced Gravity (ISS mini-book, NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

title: On Earth even a small flame makes its own 30 cm/s wind
statement: On Earth, even small flames induce a buoyant flow of no less than about 30 cm/s, so flame spread in slower flows cannot be studied; in microgravity, flames can spread in artificial flows below 30 cm/s. FLARE measures the minimum oxygen level at which flames keep spreading.

measurements.quantity: minimum buoyant flow of a small flame in 1 g

safetyImplication: Ground tests cannot reproduce the slow airflows of a spacecraft cabin, so microgravity data are needed for material ratings.

sources.title: JAXA: Fundamental Research on International Standard of Fire Safety in Space (FLARE)

title: Lunar gravity can make some materials more flammable than on Earth
statement: Lunar gravity has been found to raise the flammability limits of some materials compared with Earth: convective heat loss is reduced, yet there is enough buoyant flow to bring fresh oxygen to the flame.
safetyImplication: Moon habitats and landers, especially at 34 % O₂, may face a higher fire risk than either Earth or orbit.

sources.title: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (Zayac, Johnston, Ruff, Ferkul), NASA Glenn poster

title: A fabric that goes out on Earth keeps burning at Moon gravity
statement: SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric burns downward in air at lunar gravity (centrifuge and parabolic-flight tests), while in Earth gravity it goes out immediately after ignition.
safetyImplication: Materials judged safe by Earth tests can sustain fire in a lunar habitat.

sources.title: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (Zayac, Johnston, Ruff, Ferkul), NASA Glenn poster

title: Russian Mir tests: ventilation can turn an ignition into a fire
statement: Russian researchers on Mir reported that most solids hardly burn in zero-g without forced air, but ventilation flows can cause a fire; they proposed lowering or stopping ventilation and studied the minimum air velocity at which burning stops.
safetyImplication: Ventilation control is a fire-fighting tool, but NASA's later review warns that a fire will not reliably self-extinguish just because ventilation is shut off.

sources.title: Fire safety experiments on MIR Orbital Station (Egorov et al.)

title: The 1997 Mir fire blocked an escape route and filled the station with smoke
statement: On 24 February 1997 a solid-fuel oxygen generator in Mir's Kvant-1 module caught fire; the flame lasted several minutes, cut off access to one of two Soyuz escape vehicles and filled the modules with smoke, which life support took hours to clear.
safetyImplication: Oxygen-generating equipment is an ignition and fuel source; smoke, not only flame, disables a crew and its escape routes.

sources.title: 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir (NASA History, John Uri)

title: Pure oxygen and flammable materials made the Apollo 1 fire spread very rapidly
statement: In the 1967 Apollo 1 ground test, the cabin held pure oxygen at 16.7 psi with more flammable material than allowed; after an electrical arc, the fire spread very rapidly and killed three astronauts.
safetyImplication: Oxygen fraction and material control are decisive; higher-oxygen exploration atmospheres need strict material rules.

sources.title: 55 Years Ago: The Apollo 1 Fire and its Aftermath (NASA History, John Uri)
